opus-5.5.text:
I think force and touch are probably among the most underutilized signals in robot learning right now, and part of the reason is that we haven't quite figured out the right way to represent them, either as inputs or as outputs.

On the input side, the naive approach is to just concatenate a force-torque reading or a tactile image into the observation and hope the policy learns to use it. In practice, what we often see is that the policy largely ignores it, because vision dominates. Vision is high-dimensional, it's informative for most of the trajectory, and the moments where force really matters, like the instant of contact, insertion, or slip, are brief and sparse in the data. So the model can get a low imitation loss without ever really paying attention to touch. I think we need to be more deliberate: things like modality dropout, attention mechanisms that can switch which sensor they rely on depending on the phase of the task, or explicitly structuring the policy so that contact-rich phases are handled with a different emphasis than free-space motion.

On the output side, I think this is actually the more interesting and less explored question. Most learned policies today output positions, either end-effector poses or joint positions, and then a stiff position controller tracks them. But for contact-rich tasks, what a human is really doing is regulating force and compliance. When you wipe a table or insert a plug, you're not commanding an exact position; you're commanding something like "push this hard in this direction, stay soft in that direction." So I'm quite excited about policies that output not just a target pose but also stiffness or impedance parameters, or target wrenches, so that the learned behavior is expressed in a space that's naturally suited to contact. That also makes the system safer and more robust to small errors in perception, because a compliant controller can absorb misalignment that a stiff one would turn into a failure.

There's also a data problem underneath all of this. If you collect demonstrations with teleoperation that has no force feedback, the human operator is effectively blind to contact, so the demonstrations themselves don't contain good force behavior. Then there's nothing good for the policy to learn. So I think the progress here has to happen jointly: better interfaces that let demonstrators feel what the robot feels, or handheld data collection tools that capture the natural forces humans apply, combined with action representations that can actually express those forces.

And finally, I'd say touch is valuable not just as a control signal but as a source of understanding. Touch tells you about properties vision can't easily see: mass, friction, compliance, whether a grasp is stable. In the longer term, I'd like to see models that build a richer physical understanding of the world by fusing vision and touch, much like we do as humans, rather than treating force as just another number fed into a policy.

r001.rationale: The response discusses force sensing and force-related actions, but does not explain that a robot’s role as a force-exerting system creates a need to measure its force output.

r002.rationale: It mentions force inputs and regulating or targeting force, but does not state that the robot uses its own force state to estimate how much force to apply.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So this is a question I think about a lot, because for a long time the field, including my own work, has been very vision-centric. We treat manipulation almost as a perception problem: look at the scene, figure out where things are, output a trajectory. And that works surprisingly well for a lot of pick-and-place style tasks. But the moment you get into contact-rich manipulation, things like insertion, wiping, in-hand reorientation, anything where the physics of contact actually matters, vision alone starts to fall apart. A camera can't tell you whether a peg is jammed or just slightly misaligned. It can't tell you how hard you're squeezing something deformable.

So on the input side, I think force and tactile sensing are genuinely necessary, not just nice-to-have. The question is how you represent them for learning. Raw tactile images or raw force-torque streams are high-frequency, noisy, and pretty unlike anything in the pretraining corpora we use for vision and language models. So there's a real design question about whether you fuse them early with vision, or whether you keep them as a separate, fast reactive channel. My intuition is that the latter is often more sensible. Vision operates at a slower, more semantic timescale, telling you roughly what to do and where. Force and tactile signals live at a much faster timescale and are really about adjusting what you're doing right now. Building architectures that respect that hierarchy, rather than just concatenating everything into one token stream, tends to work better and also makes the data problem easier, because the reactive policy can be learned from relatively little data.

On the output side, I think it's underexplored. Most of our policies output positions or velocities, and then a stiff controller tries to track them. But a lot of what makes humans good at manipulation is that we don't commit to positions. We commit to a kind of compliance, a target force, an impedance. If a policy can output something like "push with this much force in this direction and be soft in these other directions," then it's much more robust to the small errors in perception that we always have. So I'd argue that the action space itself should include force or impedance parameters, not just where to move. That makes the learning problem a bit harder in terms of demonstration collection, because teleoperation interfaces don't naturally expose that, but I think it's where things need to go.

The last thing I'd say is about data. One reason tactile sensing hasn't taken off in learning-based manipulation as fast as vision has is that there's no internet of tactile data. Every sensor is different, every robot is different, and the signals don't transfer easily. So there's a real need for either standardization or for learning representations that are sensor-agnostic. I think that's one of the more interesting open problems right now, and probably the bottleneck to actually making force and touch first-class citizens in these systems.

r001.rationale: The candidate says force and tactile sensing are necessary for contact-rich tasks and explains that force signals help assess and adjust contact force.

r002.rationale: It discusses force/tactile input and force-aware actions, but does not clearly state that the robot should use its own force state to estimate how much force to apply.

astra-6.text:
I think it should be both, but they play different roles. As an input, touch tells you about the interaction that vision alone can’t fully capture. You might see that the gripper is around an object, but you still need to know whether you have a stable grasp, whether it’s slipping, or whether you’re applying too much pressure. That becomes especially important when contact is occluded or you’re doing something precise, like inserting a part.

On the output side, I wouldn’t necessarily have the policy directly command every force at every instant. It could specify a desired force, or how compliant the robot should be, and let a lower-level controller execute that reliably. The right interface depends on the task.

The interesting learning problem is how to connect those two sides: can the robot use the contact it feels to continuously adjust what it does? You don’t want tactile sensing to just be another feature that gets concatenated with an image. You want it to actually change the behavior—relax the grip, reposition, or stop pushing when the contact doesn’t match what the robot expected.

sol-6.1.text:
I think force and tactile sensing are really important because manipulation is fundamentally about contact. Vision can tell you where an object is and help you approach it, but once you make contact, you need to understand what’s happening at that interface. Is the object slipping? Are you pushing too hard? Have you actually made contact with the surface you expected?

As an input, tactile information can help the policy infer things that are hard to see, especially when the hand occludes the object. Force feedback can also let the robot react quickly to unexpected contact instead of relying entirely on a visual estimate.

As an output, I think there’s an interesting question about what the learned policy should command. You might predict a desired force, or parameters for an impedance controller, rather than just a sequence of positions. Then a lower-level controller can handle the fast contact dynamics.

The challenge is learning how to use these signals together. We shouldn’t assume that adding more sensors automatically gives us better manipulation. We need representations and training data that make the contact information useful, and an architecture that connects higher-level decisions with fast feedback during execution.

r001.rationale: The response discusses force and tactile sensing at contact, but does not explain that robots exert force and therefore need to measure their own force output.

r002.rationale: It suggests commanding a desired force or impedance parameters, but does not state that the robot should use its own force state to estimate how much force to apply.
